verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, of David, a psalm. God of my praise, do not be silent.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster. A psalm of David. O God, you are my praise, the one my whole voice rises toward. Do not be silent now.
verses.directors_commentary:
The superscription is part of the verse in the Hebrew, which is why the KJV numbers it 109:0 and opens its own verse 1 at the first line. 'Choirmaster' (lamnatzeach, from the root n-tz-ch, 'to be preeminent, to oversee') names the temple musician who led or directed the piece; the KJV's 'chief Musician' is acceptable but reads like a title of rank rather than a job. Then the voice breaks in, and the opening petition is a command to God: 'do not be silent.' In a world where the gods were thought to speak through oracle, omen and verdict, a silent god was an absent judge. The speaker is being slandered, and silence would read as consent to the slander.

The KJV 'Hold not thy peace' is archaic for the plain verb 'be silent' (the same root that gives 'deaf-mute'; compare Num 30:5 [Hebrew 30:5] 'if her father is silent'). 'God of my praise' is a compact and odd phrase: God is not only the one praised but the one whose acts are the speaker's glory, his reputation. That matters because the next verses are an attack on that reputation. Play it as someone standing in a public place, with the accusation still in the air, turning to the one witness who can answer.

philological_notes.note: 'my praise': both the praise the speaker gives and the one praised, or the glory God has given him. The same word names the whole book (Tehillim). Against the slander of the next lines, the sense of 'my renown' is strong.
'be silent', the same verb as in Num 30:5 'her father is silent'. It is a refusal to respond, not mere quiet.

verses.translation_literal: For the mouth of [the] wicked and the mouth of deceit against me they have opened; they have spoken with me [with] a tongue of falsehood.
verses.translation_dramatic: For wicked mouths have opened wide against me, mouths full of deceit. They have spoken to me with a lying tongue.
verses.directors_commentary:
The grammar is compressed and the KJV smooths it: 'the mouth of the wicked and the mouth of the deceitful are opened' makes a passive of an active verb. The Hebrew says they have opened (pataḥu, third person plural active), and 'mouth of deceit' is a mouth made of deceit, not a mouth belonging to deceitful men. Ibn Ezra reads it as a shorthand for 'a man of deceit.'

Note the two prepositions. They have opened their mouths 'against me' ('alai), but they have spoken 'with me' ('itti). The KJV again flattens this to 'against me' twice. The second preposition is the sting: these people talk to his face, and the lie is in the friendly conversation, not only behind his back. Radak and Metzudat David both hear it that way, as people who show themselves as friends. An actor should play the attackers as smiling. 'Opening the mouth' also has a physical edge: the image of a mouth gaping like a predator's, as in Psalm 22:13.

philological_notes.note: 'with me', not 'against me'. The speakers address him directly. The preposition and 'alai' in the same verse are a deliberate contrast: the lie is a face-to-face lie.

'a tongue of falsehood': the tongue is named as the instrument. The KJV 'lying tongue' is fair, but the construct 'tongue of' mirrors 'mouth of' in the first half, forming a body-part chain, mouth, mouth, tongue.

verses.translation_literal: And words of hatred have surrounded me, and they have fought me without cause.
verses.translation_dramatic: Words of hatred ring me round like a wall of spears, and they make war on me, and I have given them no cause.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Surrounded' (savavuni) is the verb of siege: it is what armies do to a city (Josh 6:3). The metaphor is military, and the next verb makes it plain, 'they fought me' (vayyillachamuni). The KJV's 'compassed me about also' adds 'also' that is not in the Hebrew; it is the translators' bridge from verse 2.

The subject of 'surrounded' is the words themselves, not the speakers, so slander is a besieging force. Ibn Ezra notes the grammar can also be read 'with words of hatred', with an implied preposition, and Radak and Meiri take it that way; I kept the literal subject, because a siege of words is the sharper picture. 'Without cause' (chinnam) is the same word as in Job 1:9, and it is the legal point: the speaker claims there was no wrong on his side that could justify the attack. Metzudat David adds that he never did them evil.

philological_notes.note: 'for nothing, without cause', from the root of 'favor' (chen): something given freely, hence 'for free' and 'for no reason'. Here the hatred is a gift no one earned.
'and they fought me', with a direct suffix, where Hebrew usually says 'fought against / with me'. Ibn Ezra and Radak supply the preposition 'with me'.

verses.translation_literal: In place of my love they accuse me, and I [am] prayer.
verses.translation_dramatic: Where I gave love, they hand me accusation. And I? I am prayer. That is all I have.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two things the KJV blurs. First, 'they are my adversaries' turns a verb into a noun. The Hebrew is yistenuni, 'they accuse me', from the root s-ṭ-n that gives us 'satan', an accuser or opponent at law. This is the first appearance of a root that explodes in the next verses (v.6, v.20, v.29). Metzudat Zion glosses it as enmity and hatred; I keep the legal edge. Second, the end of the verse has no verb at all: 'and I, prayer.' The KJV invents 'I give myself unto prayer' to fill the gap; the Hebrew is starker, and the gap is the drama.

The tradition is split on how to fill it. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat David read 'a man of prayer', and, from Psalm 35:13, that the speaker prayed for his accusers when they were sick. Others (Radak quoting his father, Meiri) take it as helplessness: he has nothing but prayer. Both are playable. I have left it as the bare equation, 'I am prayer', and the dramatic layer lets it tilt toward helplessness while the commentary keeps the other. 'Love' here is covenant loyalty to people who owed him, not romance. 'Instead of' (tachat) is an exchange word, it will repeat twice in the next verse.

philological_notes.note: 'they accuse me, act as my adversaries'. The root is legal and personal: an opponent who obstructs or accuses. It is the same root as ha-satan in v.6, so the verse prepares the 'accuser' of that line.

'and I [am] prayer': a verbless clause. Traditional readings supply 'a man of' (Ibn Ezra, Radak, comparing Ps 35:13, and Meiri comparing Dan 9:23), or take it as 'I have nothing but prayer' (Radak's father, Meiri).

verses.translation_literal: And they have put on me evil in place of good, and hatred in place of my love.
verses.translation_dramatic: They have laid evil on my shoulders where I gave good, and hatred where I gave love.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the ledger of the grievance, and its form is a double exchange: 'evil in place of good, hatred in place of love', the same preposition tachat as in verse 4. The KJV's 'rewarded' is an interpretation; the verb is simply 'put' (sim), and the preposition is 'on me' ('alai), as if loading a burden or a yoke. The Hebrew has no word for payment. They did not pay him back; they put something on him. Reading the line as a failed transaction is correct, but the picture is heavier than the KJV's.

In the ancient Near East, a beneficiary owed his patron loyalty (hesed), and a treaty partner owed good faith. To return evil for good was not just rudeness, it broke the basic reciprocity that held a community together. Meiri, Radak and Metzudat David all note the repetition and take it as emphasis. Rashi says the 'good' was the seventy bullocks that David (here reading the king as all Israel) offered for the seventy nations, and for their rain. That is a midrashic reading of the festival of Sukkot, not an obvious sense of the text, so I leave it in the notes only.

philological_notes.note: 'and they put, set'. Not 'rewarded': the Hebrew has no payment word. Evil is set on him as a load.
'in place of, instead of, in exchange for'; it appears in v.4 and twice here, making an accounting refrain.

verses.translation_literal: Appoint over him a wicked [man], and let an accuser stand at his right hand.
verses.translation_dramatic: Set a wicked man over him. Let an accuser take his stand at his right hand.
verses.directors_commentary:
From here to verse 19 the psalm turns to a series of wishes in the third person singular, and the whole psalm hangs on who is speaking them (see the reviewer note). The KJV capitalizes 'Satan', and so makes it the devil. The Hebrew has no article ('the satan') and no sign that a cosmic figure is meant: it is 'a satan', an accuser, as in 1 Kings 11:14, where the LORD raises up 'a satan' against Solomon, a human rival. Ibn Ezra reads it as a man, one of the counselors. The verb 'appoint' (hafked) is an office word, the same root as 'office' in v.8; the wish is that a wicked man be given authority over him, as a governor or judge.

The courtroom is the setting. In a trial, the accuser stood at the right hand of the accused (compare Zech 3:1 where the satan stands at the right hand of the high priest Joshua, and Ps 110:5 where the LORD is at the right hand of the king to protect him). So the right hand is the place of the prosecutor here, and the picture is of a defendant already surrounded. Malbim reads exactly this: a wicked judge, and an accuser at his right in court. The KJV's 'Set thou a wicked man over him' is right in sense, but 'Satan' changes the genre.

philological_notes.note: 'appoint, commission', an official's appointment; the noun 'office' (pequddah) of v.8 is from the same root. Metzudat Zion glosses it as the appointment of an overseer or treasurer.

'an accuser, an adversary'. Without the article it is a common noun, as in 1 Kgs 11:14 (a human 'satan' raised against Solomon), and Ibn Ezra explicitly says it is a man. The article-bearing 'ha-satan' of Job 1-2 and Zech 3 is the heavenly title. 'Stand at the right hand' is the prosecutor's place in Zech 3:1.

verses.translation_literal: When he is judged, let him come out wicked, and let his prayer become sin.
verses.translation_dramatic: When he is judged, let him walk out of the court a guilty man. And let even his prayer be counted as sin.
verses.directors_commentary:
The courtroom scene continues. 'Come out wicked' (yetze' rasha') is a verdict formula: the one who is declared in the wrong 'comes out' a rasha', 'guilty, in the wrong', as opposed to the one who comes out tzaddiq, 'in the right' (Deut 25:1). The KJV's 'condemned' captures the legal result, but the Hebrew keeps the word that has been the enemies' name since verse 2, 'wicked'. The wicked who attacked him are to get their own name back, as a verdict. Ibn Ezra and Radak take the judge to be God or an earthly court, and Rashi has the judge before God.

The last line is the sharpest. 'Let his prayer become sin' (la-chata'ah, 'into sin'): the one thing the speaker offers (v.4, 'I am prayer') he asks to be denied the enemy, and worse, reversed. Radak and Meiri read 'sin' with Judg 20:16, 'did not miss', as 'a prayer that does not reach'; Metzudat David reads it as a reminder of guilt, a prayer from an insincere heart. The Hebrew word is a rare feminine form, chata'ah, and the KJV's 'become sin' is fine, only the ASV 'turned into sin' catches the becoming (tihyeh).

philological_notes.note: 'let him come out wicked': the verdict formula, opposite of 'come out righteous'. The word rasha' also names the enemies in v.2 and the appointee in v.6. KJV 'condemned' gives the effect, not the word.
'into sin'. A rare feminine form of the noun, found here and in Ps 40:7. Radak and Meiri connect the verb 'miss' with Judg 20:16 and hear 'a prayer that misses its mark'.

verses.translation_literal: Let his days be few; his office let another take.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let his days be few. Let another man take up his office.
verses.directors_commentary:
Verse 8 is famous because Peter quotes its second half in Acts 1:20 for the replacement of Judas, in the Greek of the Septuagint ('let another take his overseership', episkope). That is the reason the KJV's 'office' sits so near to 'bishoprick' in Acts. The Hebrew word, pequddah, is wider: it is any post of oversight, a commission, a charge. Rashi reads it as 'his greatness' and compares Esther 2:3 where the king appoints officers; Radak and Metzudat David take it as the thing he is charged with, his wealth or his wife. Ibn Ezra lists a whole set of options (wife, soul as a 'deposit', or the person's fate), and Malbim reads it as a military command, 'what he had been commander of'.

The curse is the ancient pair: a short life and a replaced name. In a culture where an office was a family inheritance, losing one's post to a stranger was social death. The KJV's 'let another take' is correct. English readers may miss that 'few' days is not a vague wish: it is the opposite of the long life promised to the righteous (Ps 91:16).

philological_notes.note: 'his office, his charge'. The commentators differ: 'greatness' or office (Rashi, Malbim), wealth or wife (Radak, Ibn Ezra), or the command he holds (Malbim). Acts 1:20 uses the word 'overseership' (episkope) for it.

verses.translation_literal: Let his sons be fatherless ones, and his wife a widow.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let his sons be left without a father, and his wife a widow.
verses.directors_commentary:
The curse follows its own logic from verse 8: if his days are few, the rest comes at once. The KJV's 'children' is wrong for the Hebrew banav, which is 'his sons'; the word 'children' covers girls in English, but the Hebrew has 'sons' (though the masculine plural can include both). I kept 'sons' in the literal layer. What matters is the pair of words that define the weakest people in ancient society: the orphan (yatom, literally 'fatherless') and the widow (almanah). Both had no legal protector. The Torah repeatedly commands care for them (Exod 22:21-23, Deut 10:18), and the prophets name them the test of a just society (Isa 1:17). The wish is to make the man's family exactly the people he and his society would be obliged to protect, and then (vv.10-12) to remove that protection.

Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri add that 'fatherless' means young: the sons are still children, and the wife is a widow in the days of her youth. The grim point is that these are the most helpless possible survivors. It is an imprecation, and it is hard to hear; do not soften it in performance.

philological_notes.note: 'fatherless ones, orphans': a child whose father has died. In Israelite law the yatom, with the widow and the stranger, is under God's protection, so this curse targets exactly the group the law guards.

verses.translation_literal: And let his sons wander, wander, and beg, and let them seek from their ruins.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let his sons wander, wander without rest, and beg. Let them search out a living from the ruins of their own home.
verses.directors_commentary:
The Hebrew opens with an infinitive absolute before the finite verb, noa' yanu'u, 'wandering, let them wander': the root repeats for emphasis, and I keep that repetition in the literal layer ('wander, wander') where the KJV had to use 'continually'. The root n-w-' is the shaking of a drunk or a nomad, a drifter who has no place (it is the curse laid on Cain in Gen 4:12, 'a fugitive and a wanderer', where a related root is used). So the wish is that they lose the household that was their identity.

The KJV adds 'their bread' ('seek their bread also out of their desolate places'), which the Hebrew does not say; it only says 'and they will seek from their ruins'. The object is missing, and the line is troubled. The pointing of 'and they will seek' (vedarshu) is odd, with a short vowel under the dalet where a long one would be expected. Radak and Meiri report that the Masorah records this and argue about it; Rashi hears 'others will inquire about them' from the vowels. I take the plain sense: they search among the ruins of the home (charavot), and the house that sheltered them is now rubble. Malbim reads it as a progression from shame to shamelessness, wandering at first to places where they are not known, then begging in their own city.

philological_notes.note: infinitive absolute plus finite verb: 'wandering, they will wander', that is, 'wander and wander'. Ibn Ezra compares Ps 59:16 'they wander to eat'.

'and they will seek', with an anomalous short vowel (hataf qamats) under the dalet. Radak and Meiri discuss a Masorah note on it, and Rashi reads the vowel as a sign that 'others' ask about them. I translate 'seek', paralleling 'beg'.
'their ruins': plural of charbah, 'a ruin, a waste place'. The KJV 'desolate places' is fine, but the sense is the wreck of their own estate, as Radak and Metzudat David read.

verses.translation_literal: Let a creditor snare all that is his, and let strangers plunder his toil.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let the creditor lay his snare for everything the man owns, and let strangers strip the fruit of his labor.
verses.directors_commentary:
In an ancient village economy a loan was secured by the debtor's land, his crops and finally his children (2 Kgs 4:1, where a creditor comes to take two sons as slaves). The 'creditor' (noshe) is exactly that man. The KJV's 'extortioner' is harsher than the Hebrew, which names the lender, a man who, perhaps, charged interest, and not necessarily a cheat. The KJV also chose 'catch' for yenaqqesh, but the verb belongs to the root n-q-sh, 'to lay a snare, to strike with a trap' (the noun moqesh is a trap, which Radak and Metzudat Zion both use to explain it; compare Ps 38:13). So the creditor is a fowler, and the man's whole estate is the bird.

The second half uses 'strangers' (zarim), outsiders with no family claim, the ones inheritance law excludes, to 'plunder' (the verb baz, of war booty) his 'toil' (yegi'o, the thing earned by labor, from the root y-g-', 'to grow weary'). The KJV's 'labour' is correct, and STEPBible's 'property' is the sense by metonymy: he does the work, they take the product. Rashi gives a long tradition note tied to Jacob and Esau; I leave that as a note, not a gloss.

philological_notes.note: 'let him lay a snare for' or 'strike at'. Radak links it to moqesh, 'a trap', and Rashi gives several readings, including 'be entangled, strike'. The KJV 'catch' loses the trap.
'a creditor, one who lends on a pledge'; the same word names the creditor in 2 Kgs 4:1 who comes for the widow's sons. KJV 'extortioner' adds a judgment the Hebrew lacks.
'his toil, the fruit of his labor', the product of wearying work. Metzudat Zion defines it as wealth that comes through toil.

verses.translation_literal: Let there not be to him one who draws out loyalty, and let there not be one who shows favor to his fatherless ones.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let no one be found to stretch out kindness to him. Let no one be found to show favor to his orphans.
verses.directors_commentary:
The curse that began with the man's body (v.8) and his goods (v.11) ends with the last thing he would have: other people's goodwill. The word is chesed, not 'mercy' as in the KJV; chesed is covenant loyalty, the faithful kindness one owes a bond. The speaker had given it in v.4 ('love', ahavah) and received hatred. The verb 'draws out' (moshekh, 'one who prolongs, stretches out') is the same root as in 'draw out your kindness' (Ps 36:11 [Hebrew 36:11]) and suggests lengthening it, as a loan of kindness over time. The KJV's 'extend mercy' catches that.

The second line makes the curse inherited: 'one who shows favor' (chonen, from the root chen, 'grace') to the orphans. A father's dead name could once protect his children through his friends. The wish is that it be worthless. Radak reads the line as the end of a chain: because they beg for bread, may they find no one who will be kind. Meiri hears the first half as a creditor's mercy, a lender who would stretch out the term. Malbim hears something else: no one will repay the orphans, out of the kindness their father showed to others, with kindness of their own. Play the lines as a slow tightening; nothing is left to take after this.

philological_notes.note: 'one who draws out loyalty, prolongs kindness'. The same phrase occurs in Ps 36:11, 'draw out your chesed'. KJV 'extend mercy' is close; 'mercy' alone under-translates chesed. Meiri takes it of a creditor who lengthens the term; Malbim of the kindness the father once did, which his sons would otherwise be repaid.
'one who shows favor, is gracious'. Related to chinnam in v.3: where they hated 'for free', the wish is that no one show gracious favor, the free gift, to his children.

verses.translation_literal: May his posterity be for cutting off; in another generation may their name be wiped out.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let his line be hewn off at the root. Let one generation pass, and the next, and by the time another stands up, let no one be able to say their name.
verses.directors_commentary: Here the curse becomes concrete: in a world with no clear afterlife, a man lives on in his sons and in the speaking of his name, so to end both is to kill him twice. The actor should not shout; this is a cold, legal sentence, and the cold is what frightens. The KJV's 'in the generation following' reads as a plain next generation, but the Hebrew is simply 'in another generation' (be-dor acher), and Radak and Metzudat David take it to mean the third generation, when father and son are both forgotten, which explains the plural 'their name'. The repeated verb 'cut off' (karat) is the covenant-cutting verb, so the curse turns the language of binding agreements against the man himself; the KJV's 'blotted out' is accurate for yimmach, which is the wiping of ink or a tablet.

philological_notes.note: 'His end, what comes after him', so his posterity. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion gloss it as 'his son' and compare Daniel 11:4; the rendering 'posterity' follows them.
To wipe away, as one wipes a dish or erases writing; the same verb is used for the flood in Genesis 7:23. It names the loss of a name from memory and record.

verses.translation_literal: May the iniquity of his fathers be remembered to YHWH, and the sin of his mother not be wiped out.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let the LORD keep the ledger open: the guilt of his fathers set before him, the sin of his mother never struck from the page.
verses.directors_commentary: The curse reaches backward as well as forward. Ancient Israel thought in terms of households, so a family's debts to heaven could be carried by its members across generations, and the psalmist asks that the whole account be read at once. Metzudat David links it to the old formula 'visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children' (Exodus 20:5). Rashi, who reads the whole passage as aimed at Esau, finds the sins in the stories of Abraham, Isaac and Rebekah; that is his interpretation, not something the Hebrew says. The KJV's 'with the Lord' for el-YHWH is loose; the Hebrew has 'to' or 'before' YHWH, the picture of a case brought into court. Hebrew sets 'remembered' (yizzaker) against 'wiped out' (timmach) here, and both echo v. 13, where the name is wiped out; the man's guilt is to be fixed in memory while his name is erased.

philological_notes.note: Niphal of zakhar, 'remember', in the sense of being brought to mind before a judge, so recorded. The root returns in v. 15 (zikhram, 'their memory') and v. 16 (zakhar, 'he remembered not'), which turns the whole passage on the fact that he did not remember to be kind.

verses.translation_literal: May they be before YHWH continually, and may he cut off their memory from the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let those sins stand before the LORD without ceasing, until he reaches down and cuts the very memory of them out of the earth.
verses.directors_commentary: The two halves are one act: the sins stand before God, and because they do, the family is cut off. Radak and Meiri take 'they' to be the iniquity and sin of v. 14; the KJV's 'that he may cut off' makes this a purpose clause, which the Hebrew does not say, since it simply joins the two wishes with 'and'. Note 'continually' (tamid), the word used for the daily offering and the lamp kept burning in the sanctuary; the continual offering keeps Israel before God for good, and here the same word keeps a man's guilt before him for ill. The verb 'cut off' (karat) returns from v. 13, now with God as the subject, and 'memory' (zeker) is the very thing the man failed to give the poor.

philological_notes.note: 'Continually, without interruption', the word that names the daily offerings (tamid) in Exodus 29:38-42 and Numbers 28. Here it is the perpetual presence of guilt before God.

verses.translation_literal: Because that he did not remember to do loyal kindness, and pursued an afflicted and needy man, and the crushed of heart, to put him to death.
verses.translation_dramatic: For he never once remembered kindness. He hounded the poor and the helpless; he ran down the broken-hearted, and he did it to kill.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the charge, and the reason for all the curses above. The sin is not only cruelty but forgetfulness: he did not 'remember' to do chesed, the loyal love that a person owes to those who have a claim on him, and the whole curse is built to answer that with the same verb. In the ancient world the poor and needy (ani ve-evyon) had no one to defend them but the king, the judge or God, so to pursue them is to attack the very people the law protects. The KJV 'shew mercy' is too soft: chesed is an obligation of loyalty, not a feeling. The KJV also adds 'even' and supplies 'that he might', and ASV and YLT are closer to the Hebrew's flat, final 'to put to death' (lemotet, an intensive form that suggests finishing off a man already down). Radak reads the three terms as David describing himself.

philological_notes.note: Loyal kindness, covenant faithfulness: the obligation to act for another because of a bond. Not 'mercy' in the sense of pity.
A rare intensive (polel) form of the verb 'to die', meaning 'to put to death, to dispatch'. The sense is the deliberate completion of a killing.
'Struck, crushed of heart'; Metzudat Zion compares 'smitten of spirit' (Isaiah 66:2).

verses.translation_literal: And he loved a curse, and it came to him; and he did not delight in blessing, and it was far from him.
verses.translation_dramatic: He loved cursing, so cursing came to find him. He took no pleasure in blessing, so blessing drew away and kept its distance.
verses.directors_commentary: The KJV, Webster and BBE turn this into a wish ('so let it come unto him'). The Hebrew is in the past tense: he loved a curse and it came, he did not want blessing and it went far. Radak and Meiri explain it as a prophetic past, a way of speaking of the future as if it had already happened, as the prophets do, and that is a reasonable reading; but the Hebrew states the justice as a fact, almost a proverb, not a request. The point is moral: the curse is not something imposed from outside, because he chose it, and blessing and curse in this world are partners with the things people do, as Metzudat David notes. The sounds help: 'curse' (qelalah) is a loud, heavy word beside 'blessing' (berakhah), and the verse ends on 'far from him', the last thing he will hear.

philological_notes.note: 'And it came to him'. A narrative past with a pronoun suffix, a form that is rare and archaic (found mainly in poetry), which Radak and Meiri read as a prophetic past for the future.

verses.translation_literal: And he put on a curse like his garment, and it came like water in his inward parts, and like oil in his bones.
verses.translation_dramatic: He wore cursing the way other men wear a cloak. And now it soaks in like water, deep inside him, and sinks like oil into the marrow of his bones.
verses.directors_commentary: Three pictures, moving from outside to inside: a garment, water, oil. The curse starts as clothing, which anyone can see (and which he put on himself), then is drunk like water, then is rubbed in like oil until it reaches the bone. The sequence is the point: nothing can wash it out. Radak notes that water is what a man drinks and oil is what a man rubs on his body for pain in the bones; in a hot climate oil was both a luxury and a medicine, so the image is of something that was once pleasant and now cannot be removed. The KJV's 'bowels' is accurate for qerev ('inward parts'), but its 'so let it come' adds the wish again; the Hebrew says he put it on and it came. Note too the word 'garment' (maddo): it is a different word from the usual beged (used in v. 19), and Metzudat Zion links it to the linen garment of the priest in Leviticus 6:10 (6:3 in the Hebrew); the choice marks a close-fitting outer dress.

philological_notes.note: 'Like his garment'. Maddo is a rarer word for clothing than beged; Metzudat Zion links it to the priestly linen garment, and Malbim plays on its sound, read as 'his measure', so that the curse he measured out is measured back to him.
'Like oil'. The same word returns in v. 24 (mishemen, 'from fatness'), where the psalmist's own flesh has lost the oil that the enemy's curse now has in excess.

verses.translation_literal: May it be to him like a garment he wraps himself in, and for a belt continually he girds it on.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let it be the cloak he cannot take off, the belt he must fasten each day, drawn tight around his waist, and never loosed.
verses.directors_commentary: A return to the clothing of v. 18, now with the belt, and now the verbs are wishes again (the Hebrew changes mood here from the narrative of v. 18). The belt (mezach) is the cord that holds up a long robe, tied around the waist before work or a journey, so it is the piece of clothing a man puts on last and cannot do without. Rashi and Ibn Ezra tie the word to Job 12:21 ('he loosens the belt of the mighty'); the same noun in Job is used for the strength a ruler binds on. 'Continually' (tamid) comes again from v. 15, so the curse is as constant as the offering. The KJV 'as the garment which covereth him' is reasonable, but it misses the repetition: the Hebrew says it twice, the garment and the belt, to show the whole man dressed in it, as Radak and Meiri note.

philological_notes.note: A belt or girdle. Rashi and Ibn Ezra connect it with the verb in Job 12:21, 'he loosens the belt of the strong'. The mem of mezach is pointed with tsere (וּלְמֵזַח), which Meiri calls unusual.

verses.translation_literal: This is the wage of my accusers from beside YHWH, and of those who speak evil against my soul.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let that be the pay of my accusers, paid out by the LORD's own hand, and of all who speak evil against my life.
verses.directors_commentary: The long curse closes with an accounting: 'wage' (pe'ullat) is a worker's pay, the same word used when the law commands that the hired man's wages not be held back overnight (Leviticus 19:13, which Radak and Meiri cite). So the curse is not rage but a debt that falls due. The word for 'accusers' (sotenai) is the verb from which the noun satan comes: a satan is first of all an opponent who accuses, as the court-room figure of Job 1 and Zechariah 3 does; here the plural accusers are the people the curse of vv. 6-19 has just described in the singular. The KJV's 'adversaries' is correct but loses that legal tone. And the KJV 'let this be' supplies a wish for a verb the Hebrew leaves out; it could equally read 'this is'. 'Soul' (nefesh) in the KJV is also misleading for a Hebrew reader: it means 'my life, myself', which is why Meiri reads the speech as meaning to claim that he deserves to die.

philological_notes.note: 'Wage, the payment for a job done'; also the work itself. Radak and Meiri compare Leviticus 19:13, 'the wage of a hired man shall not stay with you overnight'.
'My accusers, those who oppose me'. Ibn Ezra reads it against 'they accuse me' in v. 4; Metzudat Zion glosses it as enemies. The root gives the noun satan.

verses.translation_literal: And you, YHWH, Adonai, deal with me for the sake of your name, for good [is] your loyal kindness; deliver me.
verses.translation_dramatic: But you, LORD God: act for me, for your own name's sake. Your faithful love is good. Rescue me.
verses.directors_commentary: The voice drops after the thunder of the curse. 'And you' is a hinge: the psalmist has said what he wishes on his enemies, and now he asks for himself, and he does not claim to deserve it. His argument is the name, not his merit, as Radak and Meiri observe: even if he is not worthy, God's name is bound up with his rescue. Malbim adds that he was anointed, so abandoning him would profane the name. The KJV 'O God the Lord' reflects the Hebrew's double divine name, which is written YHWH but pointed with the vowels of Elohim so that readers say 'Elohim Adonai' (God the Lord), as the Targum has it, and do not pronounce the name; the dramatic text renders it 'LORD God' as the natural English order. KJV 'mercy' again renders chesed, which is more than mercy. The imperatives are short and plain: 'deal', 'deliver'. Let the actor hold the silence before the last one.

philological_notes.note: The divine name written with the vowels of Elohim, since it stands next to Adonai; read as 'Elohim Adonai' ('God the Lord'), as the Targum (אֱלֹהִים יְיָ) and the KJV have it. The translation keeps both names.
'For the sake of your name': God's reputation is the ground of the appeal. Radak: even if I am not worthy, act for the sake of the name in which I trusted.

verses.translation_literal: For I [am] afflicted and needy, and my heart is pierced within me.
verses.translation_dramatic: For I am poor and I am helpless, and my heart is hollowed out inside me.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalmist now claims the very titles his enemy tormented in v. 16: 'afflicted and needy' (ani ve-evyon). The man who preyed on the poor has found one in the psalmist, and Malbim sees this answer to that charge. Whether he means material poverty or the condition of a person with no defender, the phrase is a legal appeal: God is the helper of the poor. The verb chalal is used of those pierced by a sword in battle (the noun is 'a slain man'), so 'wounded' in the KJV softens the image; the heart has been run through, and Radak reads it as killed within him. Note the form, which is pointed oddly as a verb that sounds like an adjective, noted by Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri. 'Within me' (be-qirbi) repeats the word of v. 18, where the curse enters his enemy's inward parts; the same space within is hollow in the psalmist.

philological_notes.note: 'Pierced, run through', as a slain man (chalal) is. The pointing is odd, half like an adjective and half like a perfect verb, as Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri note; they read it as a verb, 'is killed within me'.

verses.translation_literal: Like a shadow when it stretches out I have gone; I have been shaken off like the locust.
verses.translation_dramatic: I am going like a shadow when evening stretches it long, and thin, and then it is gone. I am shaken off like a locust from a cloak.
verses.directors_commentary: Two images of a life that is almost over. Rashi places the first at evening: when the sun is low, a shadow lengthens and then vanishes with the light, so it is the image of a day that is ending. The KJV 'when it declineth' is fine, but the Hebrew verb is the same 'stretch out' used of a tent or a hand. The second image is the locust, shaken off a branch or a garment and thrown about by the wind or the hand; it has no nest, as Radak and Meiri say, and goes from fence to fence. The KJV's 'tossed up and down' is loose; ninnarti is a Niphal, 'I was shaken off, driven out', and the Hebrew for locust (arbeh) is the swarming insect of the plague in Exodus 10. Ibn Ezra reads the shadow as the shortness of his days and the locust as the lack of an end to his wandering. A fine point for the director: both verbs are first person perfect and passive, so he is the one acted on.

philological_notes.note: Niphal of na'ar, 'to shake out, shake off', as one shakes out a garment (Nehemiah 5:13, cited by Metzudat Zion). He is a thing flung off, not a creature that leaves.
The locust, from the root 'to be many'; the swarming insect, driven by wind, that has no settled home.

verses.translation_literal: My knees have stumbled from fasting, and my flesh has grown lean from fat.
verses.translation_dramatic: My knees give way beneath me from fasting, and the flesh that once filled me has wasted to nothing.
verses.directors_commentary: The body bears witness. In the ancient world a fast was a public act of petition: a man starved himself in sackcloth and ashes so that God would see his pain and act (Radak). So the weak knees are not only hunger but a prayer. The KJV 'my flesh faileth of fatness' is correct in sense but archaic; the Hebrew says the flesh has become lean, kachash, 'has grown lean', away from shemen, the same word as 'oil' in v. 18. The curse sinks into the enemy's bones like oil, while the psalmist's own flesh has lost the oil it had. Malbim adds an argument: the fasting and the penance show he has no more punishment coming. And note that the enemies will mock him for this in v. 25. BBE 'for need of food' makes the fast involuntary; the Hebrew 'from fasting' (mitzom) is deliberate.

philological_notes.note: To grow lean, to fail; Metzudat Zion glosses it as thinness. The root also means 'to deny, to lie' elsewhere, but here it is physical wasting.
'From fatness, from oil'. Shemen is both oil and the fat of the body. Radak reads it as the fat the flesh had before.

verses.translation_literal: And I, I have become a reproach to them; they see me, they shake their head.
verses.translation_dramatic: And I have become the thing they sneer at. They look at me, and the heads begin to move, side to side, slow and knowing.
verses.directors_commentary: The singer is describing a public humiliation, and the staging is a street: he walks by, and heads wag. In the ancient Near East shaking the head at someone was a gesture of mockery and dismissal, a way to say that the man's fall is deserved; it is the same gesture the passers-by use against the sufferer in Lamentations 2:15. The sound plays along: the verb 'they shake' is a causative, 'they make their heads sway', and the two verbs 'they see me, they shake' come one after the other with no 'when', so that the mockery is nearly automatic. The KJV, with 'when they looked upon me they shaked their heads', adds the 'when' and also an old-fashioned past tense 'shaked' where Hebrew has a present habit. 'Reproach' (cherpah) is not a mild word: it is the loss of honour before others, the very thing the speaker has been losing since the start of the psalm.

philological_notes.note: Shame or taunt heaped on a person; here a person who has himself become the object of the taunt, as in Psalm 22:7 and 79:4. The loss is social, not only emotional.
Hiphil of nua', 'to cause to sway'. Metzudat Zion glosses it as a word of motion, and Metzudat David reads the gesture as mockery.

verses.translation_literal: Help me, YHWH my God; save me according to your covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: Help me, LORD, my God. Save me. Do it as only you do it, out of that faithful love of yours that does not let go.
verses.directors_commentary: After the mockery of verse 25, the voice turns upward, and two commands come in an escalating pair: 'help me' and 'save me'. Malbim hears the rise: salvation is more than help. The appeal does not rest on the speaker's merit but on the character of God, hence 'according to your chesed', the loyal love that a covenant partner owes and gives. The KJV's 'mercy' and the ASV's 'lovingkindness' both soften this: chesed is not pity for a stranger but faithfulness to a bond. Notice the double address, 'YHWH my God': the speaker names the covenant name and claims him as personal. In the courtroom of the psalm, this is the plea of someone who has no defender but his patron.

philological_notes.note: 'According to your covenant loyalty': the ground of the plea is God's own bond, not the petitioner's worth. Malbim notes that chesed does not look at the merit of the one who receives it.

verses.translation_literal: And let them know that this is your hand; you, YHWH, you have done it.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let them know it. Let them see that this is your hand, this and nothing else. You, LORD. You did it.
verses.directors_commentary: The speaker wants a rescue so unmistakable that nobody can explain it away. Radak and Metzudat David both make the point: the salvation should not look like chance or like the speaker's own strength. 'Hand' is the Hebrew idiom for power at work, and 'this' points at a deliverance that has not happened yet but is already being staged as a witness for the mockers. The verse ends on a pronoun doubled for force: 'you, YHWH, you have done it', the suffix on 'asitah carrying the 'it' into the verb itself. The KJV 'that this is thy hand; that thou, Lord, hast done it' is accurate, though it turns the second clause into a separate purpose, where the Hebrew simply lets the pronoun stand alone. The BBE's 'the work of your hand' replaces the idiom with a paraphrase.

philological_notes.note: 'Your hand': in biblical idiom, God's active power, especially in rescue or judgment. Here the hand is visible to the enemies as well.

verses.translation_literal: They will curse, they; and you will bless. They have arisen, and they are ashamed; and your servant will rejoice.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let them curse; they will. And you will bless. They rose against me, and look: they are shamed. And your servant, only your servant, is glad.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse is built on contrasts that the Hebrew makes audible: 'they' against 'you', 'they curse' against 'you bless', 'they rose' against 'they are ashamed', and last of all the lone 'your servant'. The pronoun 'they' is spoken out in full (hemmah) before the verb is done, which is a way of pointing a finger. Cursing in the ancient world was not just insult but a spoken force, and the speaker's answer is not a counter-curse but a trust that a blessing from God outweighs it; the Metzudat David says that God turns the curse itself into a blessing. The tenses are the puzzle: 'they have arisen and been ashamed' is perfect plus wayyiqtol, and Meiri takes the past as standing for the future, a prophetic certainty. The KJV and ASV treat it as a wish ('let them be ashamed'); the Hebrew's confidence is stronger than a wish. The 'servant' is the speaker's own humble title before his patron, the one who has no other claim.

philological_notes.note: A perfect followed by a wayyiqtol: 'they have risen and they were shamed'. Meiri reads the past as standing for the future, the shame as certain before it comes.
'Your servant': a self-description of the speaker as the dependant of God, the party who has the right to be defended by his master.

verses.translation_literal: My accusers will put on humiliation, and they will wrap themselves in their shame like a robe.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let those who accuse me be dressed in disgrace. Let their own shame be draped around them, cloak-wide, the way a man wears a robe, so that everyone sees.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm's long curse ends with a wardrobe. The speaker asks that his accusers be clothed, first in humiliation (kelimmah), then wrapped in their shame (boshet) 'like a robe'. In the ancient world, clothing announced rank and role, and a garment was a public statement: a man in the robe (me'il) was recognised for who he was. The curse is therefore that the accusers' worst quality will be as visible as a coat. Malbim reads the nuance carefully: the inner garment, worn next to the body, is private, and the outer robe is shown to all; he says the speaker asks that shame be an outer robe that others see. The word for 'accusers', soṭnay, comes from the root that gives the later noun 'satan', 'adversary'; the KJV's 'adversaries' and the BBE's 'haters' blur this courtroom sense. The KJV adds 'their own' and renders the second term 'confusion', which is not what boshet means.

philological_notes.note: Participle: 'those who accuse or oppose me'. The root is the one behind the later title 'the satan'; here it is plain human adversaries, in the same courtroom setting as the earlier verses of the psalm.
A robe or outer mantle, worn over other clothes. Radak and Meiri note the unusual pointing of the preposition without dagesh in the mem.

verses.translation_literal: I will give thanks to YHWH exceedingly with my mouth, and in the midst of many I will praise him.
verses.translation_dramatic: And I will thank the LORD, loudly, with all my mouth. I will praise him in the middle of the crowd, where everyone can hear.
verses.directors_commentary: The mood changes from the curse to the thanks, and from the courtroom to the public square. The speaker's mouth, which has been the place of slander in this psalm, is now claimed for praise: the phrase 'with my mouth' is not redundant but a deliberate reversal. 'In the midst of many' places the thanks in the assembly, which in the ancient world was not a private act: a vow of praise was a public debt paid before witnesses, as Meiri says, publishing God's wonders. The KJV's 'multitude' is accurate enough, but 'among the multitude' loses the picture of the singer standing in the middle. Two verbs for praise, 'odeh' and 'ahallelennu', belong to the language of the temple thank-offering, and the second carries a pronoun: 'I will praise him', not merely 'praise'. Malbim adds a striking thought: he reads the thanks as extending even to the trouble, since it led to the rescue.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of yadah: to acknowledge, confess, thank publicly. The same verb covers thanks and open confession, which is why it suits a testimony in the assembly.
'I will praise him', with an energic suffix; the root is the one in 'hallelujah'.

verses.translation_literal: For he stands at the right hand of the needy one, to save from those who judge his soul.
verses.translation_dramatic: For he stands there, at the right hand of the poor man, to save him from those who sit in judgment on his life.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm that began with an accuser standing at the right hand of the wicked man (verse 6) ends with a better figure at the right hand of the needy. The mirror is deliberate: the right hand is the place of the advocate or defender in a court, and God takes the very position the accuser held. The 'needy one' (evyon) is the speaker, who calls himself that in verse 22, and he has no one else. 'Those who judge his soul' is literally that: the Hebrew 'soul' (nefesh) means the person's life, so the judges are people with a verdict over his life; the KJV's 'condemn' decides the verdict in advance, and the BBE's 'those who go after his soul' replaces the judges with hunters. Malbim and Metzudat David read a literal court; Radak reads schemers who plot to kill. The text keeps both possible. The verb is imperfect, 'he stands', a habit, not a single event: this is who God is.

philological_notes.note: 'At the right hand of the needy': the place of the defender in court or of a helper at one's side. It answers verse 6, where the accuser stands at the right hand of the wicked.
'From those who judge his life': a participle of shafat, 'to judge', with nefesh as the person's life. Radak reads people who intend death; Metzudat David and Malbim, a corrupt court.
